INTERNATIONAL SITUATION SINCE JUNE 14, 1941 -Canada's war effort
The house in committee of the whole, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose yesterday I was dealing with the matter of equipment. My hon. friend the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) had asked with regard to training equipment for units. I have had the matter gone into, and I should like to give him this reply.
He asked whether there were any units in training in Canada which are lacking in essential equipment for that training, and he spoke particularly of the fifth armoured division. I think we ought to differentiate in the matter of training equipment between the training carried on at the training centres and the training carried on in the units themselves. With regard to items of armament and equipment of which there was initially, as my hon. friend and the committee know, a marked shortage, we have in general given priority to allotment to training centres. The reason
4126	COMMONS
The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
for that is obvious. It enables the utmost possible use to be made of the limited quantities of equipment for the benefit of the greatest number. As a result of that policy I can say that some time ago we reached the stage where all our training centres were in possession of essential training equipment of all types except for two or three items of which we are still deficient, and I shall mention them in a moment.
That applies to the training camps across Canada for the trainees?

To the training centres.
As regards the equipment necessary for the training of units, this, as I said, got a lower order of priority in the distribution. Nevertheless, again excepting a few items which I shall mention in a moment, the situation now is that all units of the active army are in possession of adequate scales of modern armament and equipment for training. We have, for example, ample supplies for training purposes of rifles, pistols, Bren guns, Vickers guns, submachine guns, 3-inch mortars, field artillery, mechanized transport, including universal carriers, and anti-gas equipment.
Our position regarding other items of equipment, such as wireless sets of which I have spoken more than once in the house, and supplies of which have been delayed, has recently shown a marked and rapid improvement.
The chief items in which there has been a notable deficiency are anti-tank and anti-aircraft weapons, 2-ineh mortars and modern tanks. We are now, I am happy to say, well on the way to remedying these shortages.
My hon. friend asked me with regard to the tanks at Camp Borden, and I told him that we had there something like fifteen of the old type tanks, and also a number of what we call the American tanks and that they were being extensively used for training purposes. I did not tell him what I did not know at the moment, and what has occurred quite recently, that we have now at Camp Borden over twenty of the most modern tanks as well. These tanks were built in Canada and have already been of the greatest possible value to the armoured training centres and to the units of the armoured divisions.
What is the weight of Lose tanks?

I am referring to the Valentine tank. We are also now making anti-aircraft guns, anti-tank guns, and 2-inch mortars, and issues of all of these items will be made for training purposes, we expect, within a very few weeks.
The committee will realize that we have to allot our production where it is most needed
[Mr. Ralston.!
at the moment. Training needs do get a very high priority, but it is not possible to apply the whole of our output by any means to training. Shipments have to be made overseas both for our own troops, to ensure them adequate reserves, and for other forces of the empire as well. We have to watch the situation constantly and send those weapons and equipment where they are most needed, and that is why sometimes we are slower than we otherwise would like to be in building up training equipment in Canada. I want to assure my hon. friends that while we are not at all complacent about this matter, it is clear that the great bulk of our deficiencies are now a thing of the past. Each day that passes will show an improvement, and I expect before long to be able to tell the house and the	committee	that	every	unit and
training school has every essential item, in completely adequate quantities, for training.
As I indicated to the committee, I do not propose, unless the committee desires it, at this stage to go into the matter of the various items of	equipment.	My	hon.	friend the
Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has done that. I have here a statement with regard to equipment if it is desired to ask questions on any item.
With regard to training	I could take a
good deal of the committee's time on this subject.	There has	been	quite	a bit of
discussion in the newspapers about it. But I do not propose this afternoon to deal with the various methods of training, because I feel that the best testimony to our training is the fact that the general officer commanding the Canadian corps in England has expressed his satisfaction at and appreciation of the way in which training has been carried out and the nature of the training which has been given to our troops in Canada before going overseas. Our training is, of course, progressive; men are at different stages of training as they leave for overseas; the longer they are here the more they are trained. But our training is integrated with the training overseas, so that one dovetails into the other and they go right along from the stage they reached before they left Canada to the next stage overseas.
There is complete understanding between our training officers. As I indicated to the house before the adjournment, the director of military training at national defence headquarters spent two months in England last winter going into this matter of training, ascertaining what the needs were and what methods were best adapted to ensuring the highest efficiency having regard to the tasks which Canadian troops might be called upon to perform.

The War-National Defence-Mr, Ralston
To remind the committee with regard to our system of training centres may I put on record the figures? We have at the present time in Canada thirty basic training centres. Their capacity at any one time is 22,000, and the annual output is about 132,000 men. We have 35 advanced training centres, which include officers' training centres, small arms training centres, army trades schools, junior leaders' schools, administrative schools, driving and maintenance schools, and the senior officers' course at the Royal Military College. The capacity of all these advanced training institutions at one time is 27,000 other ranks and 3,000 officers; the annual output-again- is about 132,000 other ranks and 6,000 officers. You cannot simply multiply the former figures by twelve, because the length of the course is different in different places, but that is the aggregate annual output of these advanced training institutions.
We have worked out what I think is a very complete system of interchange between England and Canada of officers and noncommissioned officers who keep in touch by going back and forth between our troops in England and our troops here.
That is for training purposes?

For training purposes, yes, and also in respect of matters to which I will refer in a minute. While this is pethaps an aside, as it does not refer to Canadian officers, I may say that there are in Ottawa at the present time twenty British officers who have come to this continent for official purposes. We have taken advantage of their presence here to have them go to our training centres and examine our training systems to see if they can give us any suggestions-and I am sure they can-with regard to the system of training which is in force there. We have the benefit of that.
Generally speaking with regard1 to training, every effort is being made to follow British experience and practice. Senior officers proceed, to Britain periodically in order to keep in constant touch with the latest training methods, and these officers return to Canada and make such alterations in our training methods as seem to be required. In addition, there is a constant interchange of officers and non-commissioned officers between Canada and the Canadian corps. This policy ensures that our training methods in Canada are in line with the requirements overseas.
Every training officer charged with training at national defence headquarters has been overseas in this war, either on a liaison visit or in actual service with the Canadian corps. The two divisional commanders in Canada,
all their senior staff officers, and many of their junior officers, in addition to a large proportion of the brigade commanders, have had overseas experience.
In connection with the schools we have these arrangements for interchange. Every advanced training centre in Canada has some officers and non-commissioned officers on the training staff who are back from the United Kingdom. There is a constant flow of personnel between the holding units in England and the training centres in Canada. That is, the holding units in England send back officers to our training centres here: we send officers over to the holding units there in order to gain experience and to integrate and coordinate the training. We are providing for-as a matter of fact orders have already been issued for-the sending to the United Kingdom of officers and non-commissioned officers from units now in Canada for attachment to units in England so that they may gain experience over there. In addition to that we have staff attachments. We send over staff officers from Canada to England, twenty proceeding at a time. In addition to that we are providing that all active units in Canada will have a certain overseas representation in their officer strength; that is to say, some of their officers will have been overseas.
May I give another example with regard to the. schools which are operating in Kingston -and there are a number of them. At Kingston, where there are four different schools, fifty per cent of all the instructors are from overseas. This applies to the three months' senior officers' course, to the three months' company commanders' course, to the four months' junior war staff course, and the four months' junior intelligence course-which is both for officers and for non-commissioned officers. The junior war staff course was started in England. Its first term was held there, and then it was removed to Canada for reasons which hon. members will appreciate, because it was regarded as a permanent institution; and as I say, over fifty per cent of the instructors at that school have had overseas service.
We have also exchanges with the British Army, apart from the ad hoc arrangement which I mentioned a moment ago, under which certain British officers now in Canada are giving us the benefit of their experience. I can assure the committee that everything that can be done to bring the Canadian training of cadets into line with modem requirements, and the experience which has been gained overseas, is being done.
I will deal with one other matter. We have, as the committee knows, officers' training
4128	COMMONS
The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
centres at Brockville and Victoria, the one at Brockville serving eastern Canada and the one at Victoria serving the west. These are organized to turn out 4,600 officers for the active army each year and to train over 2,000 officers for the reserve army each year. In addition to qualifying those already granted commissions, these schools take on for training 1,200 cadets who have been recommended and who are seeking to qualify for commissioned rank in the active army. We have also made arrangements in that connection with what is called the O.C.T.U. in England, the officer cadets training unit in the United Kingdom, so that at the end of every second course they send to us, to be attached to our officers' training centres here, two officers who have had experience instructing in the cadet training unit overseas. We keep them here for two courses and then allow them to go back, having other officers come to take their place.
I spoke of the junior war staff course at the Royal Military College for officers up to the appointment of G-2-a three months' course. Forty officers can be accommodated at one time. We have a school of army administration, providing for an administrative staff course for eight officers for four weeks; a wing for unit administration course for twelve officers, of four weeks; a wing for adjutants, company sergeant-majors and orderly room sergeants' course, eight officers and sixteen other ranks, covering two weeks; a wing for quartermasters and quartermaster sergeants, eight officers and sixteen other ranks, two weeks; and an advanced clerks' course for thirty other ranks covering four weeks.
We have a bilingual junior leaders' school at Megantic. There are fifteen courses in the year, there being two hundred candidates in each course. It is what its name implies, a course for non-commissioned officers, for junior leaders who are given special training in the responsibilities of leadership.
We have an advanced driving and maintenance school at Woodstock, Ontario. The men who go there first take what we call phase 2 training, which is training given at the technical schools which are operated under the Department of Labour throughout Canada. They then go to Woodstock and take one month's intensive course as driver mechanics. We accommodate four hundred a month, and the output ultimately will be about five hundred a month.
I cannot emphasize too strongly what I said last night as a result of what I observed overseas, namely, the importance of the work that is done by the driver mechanics. There is a great deal of work behind the lines which can

be saved if the driver mechanic is taught the principles of his trade and learns to look after his vehicle each night when he comes in, instead of allowing it to go until it gets so run down that it has to be laid up and sent to the workshop for major repairs. We give that special course in addition to some other courses for tradesmen, to which I shall refer.

While the minister is on that point, recalling the statement made in this house about a year ago, may I ask to what extent non-commissioned officers have been privileged to get commissions? It has been said that the men must all pass through the ranks before commissions can be granted, but there have been many complaints from non-commissioned officers who say that they are still without opportunity of reaching that objective. Perhaps the minister will give a word of explanation.

That would entail my getting information as to the number. My hon. friend will note what I said, namely, that at Brockville and Victoria we have no less than 1,200 cadets who are being trained during the year. They have gone through the ranks- almost all would be non-commissioned officers. They are recommended as cadets and they go to the officers' training school on that basis and obtain commissions if they pass their course.
They come principally from the non-permanent active militia.

That may be. I shall have the figures looked up to see what number of non-commissioned officers or cadets have been put through.
I did not mention, in connection with the promotion of close relations between England and Canada, the matter of commands. I need only remind the committee that the divisional commanders have all had overseas service. Practically all brigade commanders in Canada at the present time have had commands overseas. A great number of senior staff officers in the various formations have been brought back from overseas. In a word, we have endeavoured as far as possible to see to it that there shall be a very substantial proportion of the senior officers in our formation who have had overseas service and experience.
Let me now say a word with regard to tradesmen. We have to realize, as I said last night, that the army cannot indefinitely continue to draw from the ranks of civilian labour large numbers of technical qualified tradesmen without seriously disrupting industry, and we have a set-up which is now in

The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston.
operation, a very extensive scheme, for training large numbers of tradesmen required in the army. Potential tradesmen are secured by enlistment or selection from existing units. Selection boards have been set up for the purpose and they are assisted by a directorate at headquarters, which has to do with the selection of personnel for the various types of occupation needed to be filled in the army.
Is the minister speaking of Canada?
Yes.
'Will he tell us the position with respect to tradesmen in ordnance in England? I understood that there was a substantial deficiency which really ought to be filled. Perhaps he knows about that.

I do know about it, and that is one of the reasons why we have doubled and almost trebled our capacity for the training of tradesmen in Canada. The facilities in England at the particular school I saw afforded training to fit men for trades of different kinds. Some of them were in training as driver mechanics. In Canada-and that is where the supply must come from- there has been, as probably my hon. friend has heard, a certain amount of combing out of units to find men adapted for that work. We have recognized that need and it has been thrown at us by the fact that the transport equipment is getting older. Some of it has been used a year and a half, and the maintenance question is an important one. There are 18,000 motor vehicles alone, apart from armoured fighting vehicles, and therefore we have had to enlarge substantially our provision for the training of tradesmen.
All these men who go to these schools about which I am going to speak are first given what we call phase 1 training, that is the basic training of a soldier for two months. Then they go on phase 2, which are these schools I have spoken of, conducted under the Department of Labour, which were the technical and vocational schools operated by the provinces all over the country. About four thousand men are being trained in those schools at the present time. The trades being taught in the vocational schools are blacksmiths, bricklayers, masons, concretors, carpenters and joiners, clerks, coppersmiths and tinsmiths, architectural, engineering, mechanical and topographical draughtsmen, electricians, engine artificers, fitters, instrument mechanics, motor mechanics, operator signals, plumbers and pipe fitters, welders, wireless mechanics, driver mechanics, turners, diesel mechanics, cooks and painters.
At these phase 2 schools, that is the vocational schools, facilities are being extended in order to handle about 6,000 men at any one time, or an annual capacity of 25,000.
As the committee knows, Canadian industry is cooperating in the instruction of additional men in a large proportion of those trades. At the present time about 4,000 men are being given instruction in various industrial plants, and the annual output from that source is now about 1,200.
When this phase 2 instruction is completed, the majority of the men proceed direct to their units or to training centres being classed as training reinforcements. The rest proceed to the army trade school at Hamilton or to the mechanics' training centre at London for further training. At the army trade school at Hamilton, which is a busy place-I know a number of hon. members have visited it-additional instruction is given in the following trades: artificers, blacksmiths, carpenters, electricians, engine artificers, fitters, instrument mechanics, motor mechanics, wireless mechanics, welders.
There is accommodation for 2,000 men at this school and the annual output will be about 500 a month. Those are more general trades. At the other school, the mechanical training centre at London, which was opened comparatively recently, I think about four months ago, instruction is given particularly in motor mechanics, diesel mechanics and aero engine mechanics. There is accommodation there for about 750 men, with an annual output of about 2,400.
They graduate from these schools and then go to the advanced training centres of their different arms-that is to say, the ordnance men go to the ordnance training centre, the AS.C. men to the A.S.C. training centre-and there they are given further training in the military application of their trades. So far they have been learning their trade; then they are shown how to apply it to the military vehicles and equipment of which they will have charge. Men of the ordnance corps, for instance, go to the ordnance training centre at Barriefield, where the present accommodation for 2,000 will soon be increased to 3,000. This releases men for overseas as and when required. In addition to giving the finishing touches to the training the ordnance training or other schools give complete training in certain specialized ordnance trades which I have not listed. The annual output will be from 1,500 to 2,000.
Then there are training centres not only for ordnance but also for other technical corps such as engineers, signals, army service and medicals. They carry on specialists' trades-

4130	COMMONS
The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
men training in addition to completing the training of the men passed through the other schools.
To sum up, it means we have or are creating facilities for training of tradesmen in Canada which will give an annual output of about
40,000	tradesmen. These 40,000 are not all motor tradesmen but men to fit into the different trades required in the various army units. May I say that for an armoured division the percentage of tradesmen required is about 32 per cent, and for an infantry division, a percentage of about 17 per cent.
What is being done about training more efficient types of cooks throughout the army and the camps in general?

One thing that is being done which I know about particularly is at the school at Borden, which I believe has done extremely good work. I am not fond of comparing the new with the old, but I am absolutely satisfied that the cooking and dietetics in this war are greatly ahead of those in the last war.
What else, apart from Borden?

We have a chief inspector of catering and messing, Colonel Webb. Colonel Webb keeps in constant touch with the messing in all the districts. The units also have messing officers who get special instruction, and their duties are to supervise the preparation, cooking, and serving of the meals. They should see that the daily diet sheet is lived up to and that the food is properly cooked. Each district has a messing inspector specially qualified. I cannot state at the moment where there are other cooking schools. I am sure there are some in the west. Has my hon. friend some complaint in regard to cooks?

Yes, there seems to be a general feeling that good food is being spoiled in so many camps by men who have not had any training or only very limited training as cooks, perhaps before they entered the army, and who in some instances neglect to remove much of that infernal grease before serving and maybe doing injury to the health of many of our men in service.

I am very sorry and disappointed to hear that, because that is not the report that comes to me. Probably the good reports come to me, but I must say that the inspectors generally as I know them are pretty rigid in regard to the matter of rations and cooking. I see or am referred to most of their reports, and I do not get reports
(Mr. Ralston.]
such as my hon. friend suggests, indicating the existence of any general condition of the kind. I did have a bad report from one training centre. I had it investigated from the top down, or the bottom up, and the reports that came to me, from an officer who was absolutely independent, showed that the condition complained of was an exception; with the exception of the one meal in question the situation was not general at all. But I should be obliged if my hon. friend would give me particulars of any instances of the kind, because no doubt there are cases where men do not complain to the orderly officer, they may think they will get in wrong by doing it, and where some action from headquarters may help.

So far as the training of cooks is concerned, men selected in the different districts as prospective cooks are being sent to selected cookhouses at training centres and other units to receive instruction in cooking, besides going to Borden for their special training there. That is being done in our district as well as in others.

I thank my hon. friend for calling that to my attention, because he has had personal experience in connection with this whole matter.
The committee may be interested to hear a word with regard to the National Resources Mobilization Act personnel. Since the four months' training plan announced last March came into effect, there have been accepted for training 25,903. Of this number over 10,000 are still in training, 4,296 have completed their training and are actively employed in the army, and about 4,000 have been discharged on medical grounds or released to war industry. The balance, according to the figure I have here, is 8,296. I am not sure that that jibes exactly with the total I gave at first, but I think it is about right. The balance of 8,296, as of October 25, have enlisted for active service in the army, navy or air force. Of these about 5,000 enlisted in the army. That is to say the figures show that out of 25,903 trained since March 20 there were 8,296 who have enlisted.
That is about one-third.

Yes, I generally estimate it at about 25 per cent. The figures are larger than I thought they were.
The committee will realize of course that this has been a very disjointed presentation, but I am trying to deal with subjects in which the committee may be interested, and concerning which perhaps not a great deal has been said.

The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
I was glad to announce the authorization of the Canadian Women's Army Corps. That corps has been organized. At the present time it has a strength of 21 officers and 425 other ranks. It is expected that by April 1 it will grow to upwards of 2,000 all ranks. As the committee knows, this is one of the ways of endeavouring to save man-power, and I am confident that once it has got under way it will grow very substantially.
What is the intention in that regard? What are they to do?

There are four major occupations. First we have dietetics, including cooks and waitresses; then, clerks, then auxiliary services and canteen workers and then motor transport workers. These are four of the outstanding lines of occupation. The committee will understand1 that where we have to have female assistance in outlying camps or outlying areas, special accommodation has to be provided. That is being done now. I think yesterday's press contained a report of some examples of cases where men have been replaced by members of the Canadian Women's Army Corps.
Is that for service in Canada?

Yes, for service in Canada. Nothing has been done as yet with regard to services outside of Canada. We want to get it well organized first. It is a situation we cannot rush at. But the response has been good, and the appointments which have been made have, in my opinion, been excellent. I believe it will be proved that we have been wise in going slowly in the matter. We have not yet appointed a commandant of the Canadian Women's Army Corps, although I expect an announcement will be made shortly. We asked Matron-in-Chief Smellie to act as adviser with regard to organization. Her experience and her judgment and advice have been invaluable. Matron-in-Chief Smellie has travelled throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and has met women in different organizations interested. She lhas explained the needs of the army for the service they can perform. As I say, the response has been excellent. As the committee is aware, personnel are obtained through the Department of National War Services. The Department of National Defence makes requisition on the Department of National War Services, and that department sends us personnel, subject to approval by the department itself.
How are the commissions granted?

Most of the officers
appointed1 so far had had service with other women's corps of this type. They have not been granted from the ranks. It is expected that shortly we shall be able to institute the system we have in the army-that is to say, coming through the ranks for a certain period, and then being commissioned.
How are the ladies to be employed called up? Is it according to date of application? A number in my district are anxiously waiting to be called.

This is within the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services. I shall make inquiries to see whether anything can be done by the Department of National Defence with respect to those who are particularly eligible.
May I just say a word respecting the reserve army. Two or three months ago we issued instructions with regard to the reserve army, which, while somewhat changing its status, gave it a definite role in our whole scheme of military organization. We have pointed out that the reserve army constitutes an important factor in the defence of Canada and in maintaining our active army overseas. In order to meet the situations as they arise in an ever-changing war it is essential that we have the reserve army well organized, well trained and, as far as possible consistent with other requirements, well armed. Present plans do not contemplate any extensive additional mobilization of reserve units, but that possibility is to be kept in mind.
We have outlined the duties of the reserve army to be these: an operational role in the defence of Canada, when and where required; aid to the civil power in cases of subversive or other disturbances; reinforcement of the active army-that is to say, by enlisting men, and having them ready to support their active unit, if it is overseas, or some other active unit in the same territory, if it happens that that particular unit has not an active unit overseas. Then there is the possibility, in some instances at least, of mobilization.
We have indicated to them that those functions are not cited in order of importance. They are all important, and we cannot tell which one at a particular time may have to be complied with. It does make the position of the reserve units difficult; at the same time that is the situation which exists in Canada, and we cannot do otherwise than ask them to have their eyes on those four roles as the major jobs for which they were organized. We have asked that they be administered so that they may be in a position to carry out
4132	COMMONS
The War-Natioiwl Defence-Mr. Ralston
whichever function they may be called upon to perform, in view of conditions at a particular time.
Then, there was another new rule. We felt we should increase the age limit and decrease the medical category. In other words we have raised the age limit for the reserve to fifty years and decreased the medical category to category C. But we have indicated that in view of the fact that they will be taking in men who will be reinforcements, and also that in some cases there might be possibility of mobilization, they may take up to a certain percentage of A or higher category men.
What they are doing is paying special attention to training, both basic and advanced and specialized. There will also be increased issue and distribution of equipment with regard to the reserve army, taking into account, of course, the needs of the active units. It is no lip-service I am paying when I point out what a valuable contribution the reserve army of Canada and its officers have made to this war effort through at first being the backbone of the active army, being in their places and endeavouring in every possible way to train men to make them ready to enlist in active units, and doing their best to induce them to understand what their duty is when the call comes.
The officers and non-commissioned officers have been indefatigable, and the men have been most faithful in training, in the attention they have given to their work, and in then-desire to be of service. To some extent the [DOT] reserve army consists of men who because of financial or domestic or personal reasons are unable to take their places in the active army. In the reserve they are trying to do their part as best they can, so that we may release all the men possible for active duty.

The pay the officers and
men receive is still on the same basis as it used to be, is it not? It is based on the time of service in Canada?

It is on the basis of training. The basis this year is up to fifty per cent of strength, that is to say, they may receive training pay for personnel up to fifty per cent of their total war strength. That is now being reconsidered.

Are the reserve units permitted to recruit up to strength? I understand that some units on the Pacific coast are far below strength and are greatly discouraged. There seems to be something wrong with the way the reserve army is being handled.

There are some officers at headquarters who have an especially warm spot

in their hearts for the reserve army and they give it constant attention. They realize the difficulties and are endeavouring to improve their position in every way and to give the reserve the recognition which will ensure that it is used to the best advantage. Representations have been received from the west coast with regard to a unit which was recruited practically up to strength and which desired to be paid for that, number. The present rule is that they may recruit up to strength, but they are paid for training only up to fifty per cent.
Would not the esprit de corps be improved if they were paid for the full strength?

Yes, it would, and the
matter is being considered. Just before I left for England I had a talk with the army council, and I am not satisfied with the situation in this regard. The rule was made because of a lack of training equipment and because of the tremendous appeal which was being made for recruits for the active army. There were not a great number of units in which the strength was more than fifty per cent, and that figure was taken as a fair average for payment. In many units the men pool their pay; they train without pay except that it goes to the benefit of the regiment as a whole. In other words, pay has not been the absolute test of whether or not a man would serve in the reserve unit. Many have agreed that their pay should go into regimental funds.
Is there any method whereby an officer or a non-commissioned officer in a reserve unit can transfer to the active army and retain something like the rank he held in the reserve army?

If an officer in the active unit asks for a man who is qualified as an officer and recommends him accordingly, I do not think there would be any difficulty about the transfer. A man may transfer to an active unit simply by enlisting.
If a sergeant-major in a reserve unit enlisted in the active army would he have to give up his rank?
If he was commission material he would be recommended by the officer commanding for an officer's training course where he could qualify for a commission.
A sergeant would have to revert to the rank of private?
Unless the commanding officer asked for a man with that rank.

A major would have to revert to the rank of lieutenant?

The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
Neither of those ranks would be carried to the new unit as of right. If a man has the qualifications and is needed, he can be transferred.
I know of cases where a man has been asked for by the officer commanding an active unit and it has been impossible to have him transferred.
If my hon. friend will give me the particulars of any case where a man has been qualified to cover off a particular vacancy, I shall look into it.
He was qualified.
Was there a place in the other unit into which a man of his rank would fit?
Wouldn't that matter lie in the discretion of the commanding officer of the reserve unit? He would have to have the consent of both commanding officers.
The officers in both units were willing, but the district would not allow it.
I am assuming that the man was requested by the unit to which he was going, and consent was given by the unit from which he was going.

In view of what the minister has said with regard to raising the age limit to fifty years and lowering the medical category, is it not likely that the number who will enlist in the reserve army for service overseas will be greatly diminished? Is there any provision under which a certain proportion of those admitted into the reserve army will be expected to state their willingness to go overseas?

There is no such provision.
Those are the subjects upon which I think the committee would like information. No doubt there are other subjects in the minds of hon. members about which they would like me to speak and when the opportunity comes I shall be glad to answer any questions.

Will the minister give us a statement at some stage of the proceedings with regard to the position of our troops in England, and who has the last say in their disposition overseas? I understood that there was some difficulty in the early stages of the war. I consulted the Minister of National Defence for Air at one time and he endeavoured to make this clear to me, but I could not understand the situation. I think the fault was probably mine rather than his.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The legislation is not very clear.

I understand that there has been some clarification and that the position is now quite satisfactory. I should like to know just what the steps have been and what the position is now. I heard that enlistments will not be received by the department for active service in Canada.

I really hesitate to make a statement with respect to the visiting forces act. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) asked me to make a statement, which I did. I will be quite frank and say that that statement was made after I had seen the Department of External Affairs and had obtained their statement with respect to the matter. There are two expressions used, "serving together" and "serving in combination with".
Is there any difference?
There is quite a difference. If my hon. friend will permit me, I would rather look up the statement I made before.
I realize it is a technical matter.

The statute is technical and the order in council passed under it is technical. I think I can say that the last word with regard to Canadian forces going to serve outside the United Kingdom lies with the government of Canada. If they go out of England for service the government of Canada would be asked to give its consent.
They have the last word?
Yes.
Does the government of Canada undertake to act upon the recommendation of the commander of the Canadian corps, or does it exercise independent judgment and make an independent decision?

The government of Canada would give the greatest weight to the recommendation of the general officer commanding the Canadian corps. The government of Canada would have to take responsibility eventually. I was writing a note in order to get the reference in Hansard to what I said before. If my hon. friend will leave it, I shall make a statement later.
I realize the difficulty. Will the second question I asked be looked into?

No, they cannot volunteer for active service confined to Canada.
4134	COMMONS
The War-National Defence-Mr. Ralston
You cannot volunteer for active service in Canada- that is a fact. Will the minister express any reason for that policy? If he does not want to do so, I shall not press him.

I shall deal with that
later, if my hon. friend will permit me.
What I have said, Mr. Chairman, was bound to be disjointed, but I have tried to give as quick a resume of the activities of the department as I could in the short time at my disposal for preparation.
Before I sit down I want to join with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has said with regard to what we learned overseas, and to pay tribute to the morale, courage and determination of the British people. I found them, as he found them, still superb, and better prepared than they were last December when I was over there. I found them still ready to go short themselves if they thought that any other theatre of war provided an opportunity for effective use of equipment against the enemy. It is both a challenge and an inspiration to go to England and to meet those men and women and those boys and girls who have stood so much in the last year, who know it is coming again, and who are absolutely unflinching.
With regard to the course of the war I think we must remember that Greece and Crete gained time for us. Hitler's attack on Russia was thus delayed, and Russia's resistance to Hitler's attack has again delayed the invasion of Britain. We now know that we have reason for thankfulness that the invasion of Britain did not come in June or July of 1940, at a time when, as Lord Gort's dispatches indicate, the situation was serious enough.
I want to impress on the committee what has already been said but cannot be said too often. My own feeling is that the war has only just really begun, that so far all that we have done is to avoid defeat, that we still have to begin to win.
Casting up the balance sheet as of to-day as compared with a year ago, we have on the debit side Yugoslavia, Greece and Crete overrun, Russia attacked and very serious inroads made upon her. The one-by-one policy has seemed to prevail, and the juggernaut has run on. On the other side, we have that outstanding fact which I have just mentioned, namely, that the British have come through. They have proved that they can stand the blitzkrieg. There is no chance in the world of bombing ever bringing those brave people to their knees. We have Iran,

Iraq and Syria, all on the credit side of the sheet. We have United States sentiment, and not only sentiment but powerful influences and support as well, more strongly consolidated and being exerted in a more effective way than a year ago. We have growing resistance in occupied countries, which is making itself felt day by day, and we have the heroic resistance which Russia is making, to the amazement and gratification and admiration of the world. All that is on the credit side of the sheet. Hitler's dream of securing not merely military but economic domination over Russia is yet unfulfilled. He expected a rapid victory. He has not had it, and it surely must have upset his plans.
But I do want to emphasize the fact that resistance is not enough and will not bring victory; that so long as the forces of destruction continue to rage there can be no security and no peace in any corner of the world. The way to shorten the war is to have the free world with its whole resources and its total energy concentrated on the supreme task of being able to deal with Hitler in the only language he knows, and that is the language of force. Canada has its place in that great undertaking.
I am no defeatist. I believe we shall win, not simply because we say so, but because Canada along with the other democracies will stop at nothing which can effectively be done to ensure that the forces of evil shall be stamped out, that the menace of slavery shall be banished, and that free men and their families may enjoy the liberty which until this struggle began we in this dominion had somehow taken for granted. We cannot take it for granted any longer. The menace is against Canada as well as against the rest of the world.
In giving enlistment figures last night the minister said that about 105,000 had volunteered for service. They would not all be medically fit, I presume.
They are the enlistments.

What are the figures
of those medically fit?
Those are the enlistments, the number accepted.
Attested as medically fit?
Yes.

We had a case in
Winnipeg of a man wanting a medical rejection. The recruiting officer told him that that could not be granted until he had actually enlisted and been medically examined. That is why I was a little confused by the minister's figures.

The War-Air Services-Mr. Power

By enlistments I mean
accepted.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the personnel of the Royal Canadian Air Force in Canada and overseas on the 1st of November, 1941, was 89,000 odd, which brings us to approximately 90,000 to-day, the 6th of November. This is in addition to personnel attached to the Royal Canadian Air Force belonging to the Royal Air Force, the Royal Australian Air Force and the Royal New Zealand Air Force. It is also in exclusion of something like 11,000 civilians, about half of whom are taking the place of service men who have been released for more active duty. So that, all told, there are to-day under the control of the Department of National Defence for Air well over 100,000 persons.
It may be of interest to the committee if I discuss for a moment the question of manpower in Canada as it affects the Royal Canadian Air Force. The age limit for the entry of pilots-I am speaking largely of air crews, that is those who will eventually become pilots, observers, wireless air gunners and gunners, in whom we are particularly interested-the age limit for pilots is from 18 to 31; it is 18 to 30 really-those who have not reached 31. For observers the age limits are 18 to 32-those who have not reached 33- and for wireless air gunners and gunners .the age limits are the same.
The class of the population in which we are particularly interested is the class from 18 to 25 years of age, and so I have asked the officers of the department to give me some statistics regarding that class in order that I may indicate to the house and the country the approximate reserves of man-power which will be necessary to enable us to carry on our operations.
Assuming that there are in Canada to-day 177,150 males between the ages of 18 and 25 who have completed junior matriculation- the educational qualification is a most important factor in our work-and assuming that 33 per cent are physically unfit for aircraft duty, because we require a very high standard, and that 17 per cent have no inclination to fly, this would leave 50 per cent available, or 88,575.
It is impossible to estimate the number of these who have already enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force and in the other services, but assuming this figure to be 50 per cent, which I think is a little low, it will leave a pool of 38,575 available for enlistment as pilots or observers.
The educational qualifications for wireless air gunners and gunners are somewhat lower
than junior matriculation. Two years of high school will do. For the moment I am speaking only of wireless air gunners or gunners.
It is estimated that 26,000 men with complete junior matriculation reach the age of 18 each year. Deducting fifty per cent of this figure to cover those who will be medically unfit or have no inclination to fly, will leave 13,000 qualified for enlistment as pilots and observers becoming of age each year. There will therefore be a deficiency, because we will require many more than 13,000, if we take only those coming up each year. Part of this deficiency will be made up by bringing up to the required educational standards, through the medium of the dominion-provincial youth training schools and the Canadian Legion, applicants who in other respects are qualified for enlistment in this category. We also have our backlog of the 38,000, and besides, if the necessity arises, the age group between twenty-five and thirty-two, to which I have not referred, but which is in existence to some extent, although it must have been seriously depleted by enlistments already, both in the air force and in other arms of the service.
Fortunately it has been possible, and without any very great propaganda on our part, to enlist a certain number of American applicants. So that for the moment at least, though I give no guarantee of the future, and for some months to come, we have a considerable reserve from which we can draw for our aircrew requirements. During the month of July, for instance, we enlisted something near 4,000 aircrew, and at the end of the month there were about that many whose applications were in a more or less complete state and of whom we could probably get 3,000 to come into aircrew training should we require them.
I give this next figure with some reluctance, and with a warning to the committee that it may not mean all that it appears to mean. It is called "approaches", "approaches" meaning that a man has visited a recruiting centre. The total number of approaches to the Royal Canadian Air Force recruiting centres since the war started is 317,304. I do not want that to be taken to indicate that there are really 317,000. I am under the impression that, particularly in the early stages of the war, a man may have gone two or three times and have been checked two or three times. But this is continuing. Last week, for instance, the figures were something like 1,790, indicating that there is a continuing interest in recruiting in the Royal Canadian Air Force, which has not slackened in any appreciable degree since the beginning of the war.
Total medical examinations at recruiting centres since the beginning of the war were
4136	COMMONS
The War-Air Services-Mr. Power
153,277. I am sorry to say that I have not the figures indicating how many of these were rejected. The total trade tests were 97,145, of which 41,896 have been enlisted. Sometimes the trade tests are only interviews with the trade tests officers, but they are all counted in here as trade tests.
I give these figures to show that, in any survey of actual or potential man-power in Canada, having regard to the requirements of the armed forces, the needs of the Royal Canadian Air Force must be taken into consideration. Particularly there is that field of the age group between 18 and 25, wherein, without any particular efforts on our part, without any propaganda, there will undoubtedly be priority for the Royal Canadian Air Force. Whether we like it or not, whether we take any other steps, selective or otherwise, the young men of Canada between 18 and 25 want to join the Royal Canadian Air Force; and it does not matter what we do about it, they are going to join it anyway.
Or the navy.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Or the navy. We have been asked by the leader of the opposition what is our objective. In so far as the air force is concerned the sky is the limit. We will take as aircrew all the young men of Canada who are willing and able to serve, and we make no limit anywhere. I do not even follow the example of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence for the Army. If anyone wants to enlist in our air force, whether his employer likes it or not, whether his employer calls him a key man or not, if he wants to come in the air force he comes in, and that is all there is to it.
With respect to the higher strategic aspects of the war which were discussed by the leader of the opposition and the Minister of National Defence, namely as to with what particular branch of the service the war is eventually to be won, I am not prepared to discuss that, because I do not know. But I will say this: you may need the army to win the war, but you will lose the war without the air force. That has been patent to everybody since the war started, and that condition is going to obtain to the end of the war. The experience of this war has shown that, even with her mighty mechanized forces, Germany made no advances whatsoever until she obtained air superiority. If one were to assimilate this factor to what has occurred in ages gone by, probably you would recast the somewhat blasphemous expression attributed to Napoleon, that God is on the side of the heaviest battalions, and say that this war has shown that Providence is on the side of those who

have air supremacy. Up to this time there has been no doubt of that.
As is usual in discussing matters relating to this department, for the sake of clarity I have endeavoured to divide the activities of the department into home war, joint air training plan, and the overseas forces.
Beginning with home war, activities during the summer recess have been confined largely to the construction of new defensive aerodromes and to the consolidation of those already started: on the east coast, Yarmouth, Shelburne, Dartmouth, Sydney; and in Newfoundland, Botwood, Gander, arwj Torbay- the latter recently opened officially by the unofficial landing of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence on his arrival from the other side only last week, in the first aeroplane to land at that particular aerodrome. Going north, we have established aerodromes and staging facilities at Goose Bay-that is Northwest River, Labrador, and elsewhere. These are for defence, for ferrying, and for spare aerodromes in case fog or weather conditions make any of the other places unavailable.
On the west coast we have carried out the same programme of developing stations all along the coast-Alliford Bay, Ucluelet, Tofino, Coal Harbour, Bella Bella, Prince Rupert, and, on this side of the mountains, of developing the great circle route Edmonton-White Horse-Alaska. The squadrons on both coasts have been materially increased in numbers, and above all we now have a certain number of aircraft for them-Digbys, Hudsons, Boling-brokes, and Stranraers made in Canada, and, recently, Kitty Hawks and Catalinas. In that respect, let me repeat what was said in the house, I believe in June, 1940, or earlier. So far as we are concerned, the first line of defence of this country is on the other side, and if we have here aircraft that are required over there they will get them. Recently we were about to take delivery of a certain number of Aerocobras, the fastest fighting aircraft in the world, but they were more useful on the other side and1 they were sent there. Only two or three weeks ago delivery had begun of a certain number of Catalina PBY flying boats, the latest and best development in this type of aircraft. They were found to be more useful on the other side and they are there now.
With respect to the personnel of these squadrons on both coasts, they have a risky, dirty, tiresome and boring task. They may not have all the risk, but certainly they have a large proportion of the risk encountered by those on active service. They serve in lonely places and in dirty weather and patrol work is hazardous in the extreme. Little glamour

The War-Air Services-Mr. Power
is attached to it, and yet they carry on day after day without complaint. I therefore wish once more to pay tribute to them and to assure them that, as circumstances permit, it will be my intention to give them an opportunity to do t'he kind of work overseas which all of them desire to engage in.
In connection with the home effort, we have instituted a school known as the CWAAF- the Canadian Women's Auxiliary Air Force. In that connection we have taken a different attitude from my hon. friend, in that, with the exception of three or four commissions, no commissions have been given directly. One commission was given the commanding officer, Mrs. Walker, and two others were female medical doctors who have come into the service with commissions. The remainder are being trained at the school in Toronto, where we have taken over the Havergal ladies' college. We began by selecting for training, to be turned out in accordance with the marks obtained, either as non-commissioned officers or officers, 150 women from across Canada. When these have been selected they will form the nucleus of the officers and non-commissioned officers of the corps, and we expect to open training schools for others, who will come in very much greater numbers as time goes on.
How do they propose to make these selections?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The 150 have been selected. The board was composed of the commanding officer, a medical officer, Doctor Davey of Hamilton, one officer who was lent to us by the United Kingdom from the W.A.A.F., and one male officer of the Royal Canadian Air Force. The board received applications in the different sections of the country and from among those applications selected those who were to go to this school for training.
What will be their principal duties

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Largely clerical and dietetic, perhaps more in connection with motor transport and more active work at the aerodromes. For instance, at the flying training schools such as Uplands, we shall require 126 to take the place of men. They will serve as cooks and so on, and do the work of service men who are employed operating telephones, and they will engage in parachute packing and work of that kind. In the Royal Air Force an infinite variety of work is being done by these women, and we expect that as time goes on, more gradually than would have been the case on the other side, it will be possible to introduce women into a great deal of the work now done by general-duties men or by men in orderly rooms on the station.
Is there a flood of applications?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We do not get the applications. I was surprised to hear the Minister of National War Services say that he had only 16,000 applications altogether from women. I surmise the reason is that women who are in existing unofficial organizations probably prefer to remain in those organizations in the hope that they will be taken over as a whole. I am only surmising that; I do not know. If so, that may account for it. I had anticipated such a flood of applications as would render it difficult to deal with the matter.
In addition to the organization of the women's auxiliary corps, the air cadet league of Canada has been instituted. It was inaugurated in June and began its work some time ago. I have here a list of the directorate. The president is Mr. George B. Foster, K.C., of Montreal, and there is a list of excellent men chosen from all over Canada. I will put the list on Hansard.

At the present time there are in existence in Canada something like 14,000 air cadets in units divided somewhat as follows-I will give the number of air cadets: British Columbia, 2,500, nineteen units; Alberta, 1,200, eleven units; Saskatchewan, 2,400, eighteen units; Manitoba, 700, three units; Ontario, 1,000, eight units; Quebec, 5,000, thirteen units; Nova Scotia, 200, three units; Prince Edward Island, 100, two units.
This is the potential which they have at the moment, because most of these units are in process of organization and have not yet applied for affiliation to the league. Actually enlisting under their auspices or belonging to the league are 3,400 cadets in thirty-three units. These 3,400 are actually affiliated to the league but the others are outside the league,

The War-Air Services-Mr. Power
though it is expected that they will come in. The league is rapidly organizing cadet units across Canada.
Is there an age limit?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The age limit is eighteen- well, they must not have reached eighteen because by that time we take them for the R.C.A.F. They can start at twelve, but those from twelve to fourteen are not encouraged.
Fourteen to eighteen?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They have the right to go
down to twelve, but we are not encouraging that; the ages that are encouraged are from thirteen to seventeen. I am glad to say that in many instances former Royal Canadian Air Force or fleet air arm officers have turned out gladly to help these boys by giving them their drill and training. The air cadet training programme is a basic training programme and is similar to the elementary ground training received in our own schools. In addition to that we have inaugurated a system of university training for future air crew recruits. It is not a C.O.T.C. in that we do not give or promise them commissions, but it is a university air training course. A number of Canadian universities have made arrangements with us to provide what is called pre-flight training on the Royal Canadian Air Force syllabus as an alternative to army training. Only university students who can meet the medical requirements for air crew training and who sign a statement of honourable intention to join the Royal Canadian Air Force at the completion of their university course are being accepted. Medical examination and uniforms will be provided by the Royal Canadian Air Force, which will also make available the necessary training equipment and instructional assistance.
Students who have completed compulsory military training may complete the air force course this year, and other students who have not yet undergone compulsory military training may spread the air force course over two academic years. Students completing this course will be recognized as having fulfilled the requirements under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
The course will be equivalent to the course of training at initial training schools of the Royal Canadian Air Force in connection with the British commonwealth air training plan. Such schools provide preliminary ground training for future pilots and air observers. The university course will provide 200 hours of similar instruction in mathematics, armaments, air force law, airmanship, theory of flight,

et cetera and will be followed by two weeks of summer camp at one of the service flying training schools, where this ground instruction in air force life will be continued under service conditions.

They will still have to
attain the educational standard?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
By the very fact of being
students at the university they have matriculation.
Besides this, in an endeavour to salvage those who have failed on their first attempt, we have opened a "cease training" school at Trenton, Ontario, for pilots particularly who fail through no fault of their own, perhaps on account of physical defects or because they just naturally cannot fly a machine. We have formed a reorientation school, or rehabilitation school if you like, at Trenton, wherein these young men are assisted in finding some other trade. It may be a man would not make a good pilot but has the educational qualifications to be an observer, or it may be a regional control officer, or if he has a good educational background he may make a ground navigator instructor, if he has a good knowledge of mathematics. I am glad to say, and I know it will be of great interest to the committee to know that that school has been placed under the care and command of one of our colleagues, who is doing a mighty good job, Wing-Commander Denton Massey, at Trenton.
After these boys are "washed out" as pilots, as I believe it is called, do they all go to this school to be re-selected for some other branch of the service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, I think so. There is
quite a number there at the present time, and at one time until they got properly organized, they stayed there some considerable time, but I am told that that situation has improved enormously and we are getting them out to other branches and other trades. My information is that this school has been a great success.

Will the
minister ascertain whether it is compulsory for these boys to go to that school, or have they the right of election?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We have had two or three kinds of enlistment; the original enlistment for aircrews I think gave us the right to say, "Even if you do not succeed as a pilot you will have to go on and try as an observer or a wireless air gunner or gunner if we want you

The War-Air Services-Mr. Power
to." As a matter of fact we did that. I shall have to check back to see what the status is of a man who enlisted for aircrew and failed on one or more points, whether we can put him down to standard duty. I think that lately we have brought that into effect, but I am not sure.
I come now to the joint air training plan. The growing importance of this plan I think I need not stress, but as an example of the interest with which it is being regarded on the other side I call attention to the fact that it was thought of sufficient importance for a member of the royal family, His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, to visit the air training
schools of the joint empire training plan in Canada, as well as those belonging to the Royal Air Force. He came as an air commodore in the Royal Air Force and, as befits such an officer, he flew from one end of this country to the other and visited as many schools as, if not more than, any inspector excepting the inspector-general of our own Canadian force. He was well received by our people; they were extremely glad to see him, and when he left he told me he had enjoyed his visit very much.

Now this I am sure will be of interest to hon. members; all the flying stations in Canada are now selected. I am not asking for any more aerodromes. As far as the joint air training plan is concerned they are not all open, but they are all selected, and I am handing to Hansard a list of the British commonwealth air training plan establishments.
